newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich penalty decision raises new questions.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich penalty decision raises new questions.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich hoped to put his political woes to rest Thursday by paying a $300,000 ethics penalty with a personal loan, but the move sparked fresh attacks from Democrats because the loan came from Bob Dole.

Worried Republicans were clearly relieved by Gingrich's surprise announcement. Some had feared a political meltdown if the embattled House leader had set up a legal defence fund or dipped into campaign money.
But the surprise announcement that Gingrich had secured a personal loan from former Republican presidential nominee Dole for the full amount raised fresh questions.

"Is this just another example of business as usual, where politicians and lobbyists work out a deal which no one else in America could get?" asked Michigan Democrat David Bonior, Gingrich's staunchest critic. "It's the good old boy network."

Democrats challenged the propriety of the loan, which does not obligate Gingrich to pay the 10 percent interest or principal for eight years. The speaker has not yet offered collateral aside from a life insurance policy to secure the $300,000.
Further, Gingrich plans to retire from Congress in 2002, years before the loan comes due.

Accusing Democratic critics of suffering from "obsessive Gingrichism," Republicans called the decision the most honourable option. They said if Gingrich had taken out a commercial loan Democrats would have called it a conflict of interest, since Congress plans to rewrite banking laws.
"This is the highest standard. (Dole) is a person who is above reproach in America today," said New York Republican Representative Bill Paxon.
Gingrich has asked the House Ethics Committee to review the loan. "He's (Dole) going to get a good commercial rate and he's going to make money," Gingrich told reporters.
Banking consultant Bert Ely called the loan an "unusual" one many banks would likely not approve. But he said it was defensible based on Gingrich's future earnings ability.

"Gingrich is more in the category of (golf champion) Tiger Woods in terms of income potential," Ely said. "I don't think he got a sweetheart deal from Dole. There's a flexibility in this you see in a lot of family loans."
Ely said if Gingrich had taken out a 10 percent commercial loan, due monthly over eight years, he would be paying about 32 percent of his income or roughly $54,500 a year.

The House voted 395-28 in January to reprimand Gingrich for using tax-exempt funds to promote political goals and misleading House investigators. He was also required to repay $300,000 in taxpayer costs expended by House investigators.
The beleaguered speaker has struggled to regain his political footing since then.

By turning to Dole, however, Gingrich may prolong the political scrutiny. Lawmakers close to the process said if Gingrich had taken out a normal commercial loan the House Ethics Committee likely would have accepted it with no problem.
The new arrangement, however, raises questions for several reasons, including House rules that bar gifts to lawmakers. The loan will be examined to ensure it is in no way a gift.

Democrats say the situation is further complicated by the fact Dole, the former Senate majority leader, recently joined a prestigious Washington law firm that represents clients with a number of thorny issues before Congress.
Dole is not a registered lobbyist. The client list of his firm, Verner, Liipfert, Bernhard, McPherson and Hand, includes major defence firms and other big industries.

"The speaker of the House is in hock to one of the principals of the tobacco fight," charged California Democrat George Miller, referring to a front page USA Today article Thursday mentioning the firm's ties to the tobacco industry.
House Majority Leader Tom DeLay, a Texas Republican, said he was shocked Democrats would attack Dole, "an American patriot whose integrity has never, ever been questioned."
Some analysts said despite the rhetoric, they expected the issue to quickly die down.

"I think it's going to be the source of a lot of fun by late night comics for the next 72 hours. After that, I'm guessing that he will have finessed it and put it to rest," said Thomas Mann, a Brookings Institution analyst.
